title: What agentic workflows require of people and organisations · hancrafted
description: What an agent and an agentic workflow are, how far a person can step out of the loop for each task, the skills each person needs (plan back from the goal, agree contracts at the seams, review the result), and what the organisation must provide so the workflow is designed around the goal, not the org chart.

What an agentic workflow is (1/2) Page 1 of 2 What an agent is An agent is a language model that uses tools in a loop and decides for itself how to reach a goal. Explain Managing effort Productivity increase Adoption AI disciplines Oversight ▶ Play all 2022–23 Chat You write, the AI answers. The entry point. Click: definition Definition : Chat is a conversation with the model: you write instructions, it answers, message by message. Source : OpenAI, prompt engineering guide ↗ ( opens in a new tab ) Draft the party invitation in 3 lines. Sure: 1. … 2. … 3. … Chat a conversation: you write, it answers, message by message 2024–25 Agents The AI uses tools and works in a loop. Click: definition Definition : Agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, keeping control over how they accomplish tasks. Source : Anthropic, Building effective agents (2024) ↗ ( opens in a new tab ) done Plan the party trip. Open the web Search trains 5 routes, fastest first. Harness the software around it: permissions, tools and a loop until done 2024–26 Workflows Several agents, step by step, to a plan. Click: definition Definition : A workflow chains model and tool steps along a path fixed in advance. Source : Anthropic, Building effective agents (2024) ↗ ( opens in a new tab ) Flowchart a graph of agents with a human in or on the loop 2026 → · emerging Factory? Agents run the lifecycle, spec to release. People pass the gates. Click: definition Definition : A factory runs the whole development lifecycle with agents, from specification to release; people set the goals and pass its gates. Source : Shapiro, The Five Levels (2026) ↗ ( opens in a new tab ) ? What an agentic workflow is (2/2) Page 2 of 2 What an agentic workflow is A structured process in which AI agents make decisions, take actions and coordinate tasks, with minimal human intervention. You design the path; the agent steers inside its task. You design this the stages, their order, what each hands over, where you sign off Use case : Plan a summer party Stages Jobs Practice it for Plan Plan → a plan of epics Get interviewed, then a short plan of epics Practice it for Requirements Requirements → tickets you signed off Grill one epic, then sign off its tickets checked You sign off Practice it for Research Research → research, a source per number Research 1 Research 2 One fresh chat per ticket Practice it for Page Page → one page: the party plan Gather it, then one page to sign off You sign off Explore it → → a plan of epics → tickets you signed off → research, a source per number → one page: the party plan The agent steers this Agent You set its task: research each ticket in its own fresh chat, with web search and a source for every number. How it gets there is its own call. Search the web → Compare 3 venues → Note a source per number until it thinks it is done “Minimal human intervention” Here you sign off twice. How minimal, and for which task? The next Section answers it.
How far you step out How much of a person stays in is a choice you make per task. in on out Food & drinks Venue kitchen a person on the loop checks the menu

How far you step out (1/2) Page 1 of 2 In, on or out of the loop Three levels of human oversight, set per task: the same workflow keeps a person in for one task, on for another and out for a third. Chosen per task In the loop Human in the loop · HITL The agent acts only after a person approves. The gatekeeper approves each step On the loop Human on the loop · HOTL It acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. The pilot watches, steps in on exceptions Out of the loop Human out of the loop · HOOTL It acts without any person, who sees only the result. The auditor checks the logs afterwards One task, three ways Venue · Book a venue for 200 on 20 June Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely Agent In the loop Proposes a venue Nothing is booked until you say yes. Agent On the loop Books the venue and reports You read the reports and step in if something looks wrong. Agent Out of the loop Books the venue You get the confirmation. Risk of a wrong result: highest where a person approves Speed highest where nobody waits Borrowed terms The words: military policy on weapon autonomy, 2012 The concept: supervisory control in aircraft

How far you step out (2/2) Page 2 of 2 Trust lets you step out; review builds the trust A task steps out only as far as the trust it has earned covers the trust it needs; a check built in is what earns it. 1 Engineer for review 2 Earned trust 3 Step out In On Out Summer party · each task steps out as far as its earned trust covers what it needs Agent Guest list 200 names, 5 offices Trust needed: a name missing, fixed with one email Trust earned: Checked by: count against each office's staff list, no person needed Out of the loop 200 guests Agent Venue A venue for 200 on 20 June Trust needed: 200 people at a place that doesn't fit Trust earned: Checked by: capacity, date, access, read in the reports On the loop venue, date Agent Activity One activity for 200 Was: Paintball × 200, only your yes or no Trust needed: colleagues left out of the day Trust earned: 2 (was 1) 3 In On the loop 1 Its check, built in Everyone can join Wheelchair access No fitness needed A test the result can pass, set before the agent starts. programme Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely My hypothesis: weighing risk and earned trust together is a synthesis, not one source's rule ( ) , and the evidence that checks build trust comes mostly from software ( ) .

What it requires of each person Four failures, three missing skills, and each skill has a name. Food & drinks Venue kitchen Receives 200 guests, 31 vegetarian Delivers dinner for 200, 19:00 Checked by menu vs definition = no meat, fish or eggs

What it requires of each person (1/3) Page 1 of 3 Plan back from the goal Backward reasoning starts from the goal and breaks it into what must be true before it, until it reaches where you stand today. Must be true before that Must be true just before Start here Venue Alpine hut, 1,800 m External The hut’s kitchen Not yours to change Subgoal Everyone celebrates together New Shuttle back after the open bar The drivers can drink New in guest info Bring warm clothes, 6 °C at night Nobody arrives cold Subgoal Everyone gets home safely Goal, as an outcome 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely State the goal as an outcome. It tells you when you are done. Mark what is outside your control. Plan around it. Find the tasks nobody owned. They appear under their subgoal. Well known Project management: the backward pass of the Critical Path Method schedules back from a fixed completion date ( ) Agents: they do better with a clearly defined goal and outcome ( ) ; left unstated, it costs accuracy ( )

What it requires of each person (2/3) Page 2 of 3 Contracts at the seams Design by contract: cooperation rests on contracts that state each party’s obligations and benefits. Agree what a task receives and delivers, not how it is done inside. Food & drinks Agent Dinner for 200, 31 vegetarian Orders from the venue’s kitchen Contract · Food & drinks → the venue’s kitchen The seam Receives 200 guests, 31 vegetarian, defined as no meat, fish or eggs Delivers Dinner for 200 at 19:00 Checked by The menu against the definition How: the kitchen’s choice Each line belongs to one side: Food & drinks guarantees what goes in, the kitchen what comes out ( ) Kitchen Person The venue’s, at the alpine hut External: not yours to change Dinner 19:00 31 vegetarian plates, no eggs

What it requires of each person (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Reviewing the result Verification checks a result against its contract; validation checks it against the goal. The second check is the human part. Activity Agent Paintball × 200 Delivered, ticked on the board One result, checked twice 1 · Verification “Am I building the product right?” ( ) Against its contract Activity for 200 Within budget On 20 June Passes: 3 of 3 2 · Validation Person “Am I building the right product?” Against the goal: everyone celebrates together Ten colleagues use wheelchairs As Travel’s accessible bus for ten already said Right about what was asked, wrong about what was needed The fix lands in the contract Checked by: everyone can join, wheelchair access Fails the goal
What it requires of the organisation The workflow people draw takes the shape of the organisation. Venue team ×10 Food & drinks ×1 seams follow the goal Activities Travel Venue Food & drinks Goal

What it requires of the organisation (1/4) Page 1 of 4 The org chart trap Conway’s law: what people design copies who talks to whom, and a workflow people draw for themselves is a design too. Party committee · org chart Committee lead Venue scouts 10 people Caterer 1 person Travel planner 1 person copies Their draft AI workflow Venue scouting · 14 steps 1 Brief the scouts 2 List regions 3 Long-list venues 4 Call 40 venues 5 Check dates 6 Visit north 7 Visit south 8 Score venues 9 Compare prices 10 Second visits 11 Shortlist 3 12 Present 13 Vote 14 Book venue Catering · 1 step Order 200 meals Travel · 1 step Book trains Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely No step plans back from here. “Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization’s communication structure.” Melvin Conway, 1968 ( ) A tendency, not a rule: strong in 70% of firm studies ( ) Applying it to workflows is my inference, not a measured result. The first design is rarely the best: redraw it from the goal ( )

What it requires of the organisation (2/4) Page 2 of 4 Designed AI first Start from the goal’s outcome, put a contract on every milestone, and cut the seams that produce nothing anyone can review. Before · the committee’s draft, 16 steps Venue scouting · 14 Catering · 1 Travel · 1 shaped by the org chart After · redrawn from the goal: 5 notes, a contract on every arrow agent Travel + guest info, merged 3 Delivers route, times, accessible bus, warm clothes for 6 °C Checked: info against the venue agent Venue: alpine hut, step-free Delivers address, step-free entry Checked: a person, at a checkpoint ( ) agent Food & drinks for 200 Receives 31 vegetarian: no meat, fish or eggs Delivers dinner for 200 at 19:00 Checked: the menu against the definition How: the kitchen’s choice 2 person Activities everyone can join Delivers a programme for all 200, step-free Checked: against the goal agent Shuttle back after the open bar Delivers everyone home, nobody drives Checked: shuttle list against guests Goal 20 June: everyone celebrates together and gets home safely 1 Outcome: 200 guests from 5 offices, all home safe 1 Start at the outcome. Roles say who is free; the outcome says what is needed. 2 A contract on every milestone , the inside left free ( ) . 3 Cut seams. Merge steps that produce nothing reviewable ( ) . You didn’t need more meetings. You needed contracts.

What it requires of the organisation (3/4) Page 3 of 4 What did you need to do? Build three skills in each person, which fix the four failures from the board, and give them an organisation designed around the goal. In each person Break the work down from the goal Carpools + open bar a shuttle back, nobody drives 1,800 m in summer clothes guest info: warm clothes, 6 °C at night Write the contract at the seam “31 vegetarian” got egg dishes defined: no meat, fish or eggs Review against contract and goal ( ) Paintball × 200 an activity the ten wheelchair users join From the organisation Clear goals An outcome you can measure, like “everyone home safe”. Contracts between teams Receives, delivers, checked by, at every seam. An oversight policy per task In the loop On the loop Out of the loop Workflows around the goal Not around the org chart. That these three are the skills to build is a synthesis: no study tests them as a set ( ) . Juniors learn them on narrow tasks, the ones agents take first ( ) .

What it requires of the organisation (4/4) Page 4 of 4 From article to quiz One whole agentic workflow turns any knowledge article, a PDF or a URL, into a quiz: each step in, on or out of the loop, a contract at every handoff. 3 Goal: a quiz someone can use Use case : Plan a summer party Stages Jobs Demo mode Practice it for Plan Plan Get interviewed, then a short plan of epics In the loop 1 Plan → Requirements Receives a goal and its epics Delivers one epic chosen Checked by: you name the epic to start 2 Practice it for Requirements Requirements Grill one epic, then sign off its tickets checked Gate 1 In the loop Requirements → Research Receives the epic Delivers tickets, each with a question Checked by: your sign-off Practice it for Research Research On the loop Research 1 Research 2 One fresh chat per ticket Research → Page Receives one ticket Delivers facts with sources Checked by: sources open and match Practice it for Page Page Gather it, then one page to sign off Gate 2 In the loop 4 Explore it → You design the path; the agent steers each step 1 Pick one recurring process. Mark each step: agent or person, in, on or out of the loop. 2 Write the contract first. What the task receives, what it delivers, how someone else checks it. 3 Suspect Conway’s law. If the workflow mirrors how people work today, redraw it around the goal. 4 Build three skills. Breaking work down, writing clear handoffs, reviewing an agent’s result.

A thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

The thought experiment A real version of the board Anthropic's lead agent gave its subagents vague task descriptions, and they duplicated each other's searches and left gaps until each task carried an objective, an output format, tool guidance and boundaries; one team's account of its own system, not a controlled comparison 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Now with agents A model can learn from public text alone the LLaMA authors set out to show state-of-the-art models can be trained using publicly available datasets exclusively 1 . Sources (1) Touvron et al., LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Customer conversations are not training data Anthropic states that by default it does not use inputs or outputs of its commercial products for training, so a company's internal processes, decisions and naming are mostly absent from what a model learned 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Is my data used for model training? (commercial products) ( opens in a new tab ) privacy.claude.com Rare facts are learned poorly accuracy on a fact question tracks how many training documents mention it, so even a fact that is in the data is weak when it is rare 1 . Sources (1) Kandpal et al., Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The context must be supplied the retrieval literature's remedy is to pair the model with a searchable memory consulted at request time, which is why organisational knowledge has to arrive with the request 1 . Sources (1) Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org
What an agentic workflow is No speaker notes for this Slide.

What an agent is Anthropic's definition Agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, keeping control over how they accomplish tasks 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com A shorter form “An LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal”, with a stopping condition 1 . Sources (1) Willison, I think “agent” may finally have a widely enough agreed upon definition ( opens in a new tab ) simonwillison.net

What an agentic workflow is IBM's wording “Agentic workflows are AI-driven processes where autonomous AI agents make decisions, take actions and coordinate tasks with minimal human intervention.” 1 Sources (1) Gutowska and Stryker (IBM), What are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) ibm.com Salesforce's wording “Agentic workflows are structured processes where AI agents make decisions, solve problems, and perform tasks with minimal human input.” The word “structured” is Salesforce's; “coordinate tasks” is IBM's. The Slide's sentence merges the two and belongs to neither vendor 1 . Sources (1) Salesforce, What Are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) salesforce.com Why the vendors stress autonomy Both sell agent platforms and praise reduced oversight; that this explains their wording is an inference, the pages give no reason 1 . Sources (1) Gutowska and Stryker (IBM), What are Agentic Workflows? ( opens in a new tab ) ibm.com Two levels of control Anthropic draws the line at who controls the steps: workflows are orchestrated through predefined code paths, agents direct their own process. Applying “you design the path, the agent steers inside its task” to a team's process is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Autonomy as a degree Ng prefers to call systems agent-like to different degrees, with a gray zone, over a binary 1 . Sources (1) Andrew Ng, The Batch issue 253 (letter on agentic workflows) ( opens in a new tab ) deeplearning.ai
How far you step out No speaker notes for this Slide.

In, on or out of the loop Origin of the three terms the triad comes from a 2012 report on weapon autonomy: in the loop means force only with a human command, on the loop means under a human operator who can override, out of the loop means without any human input 1 . Sources (1) Human Rights Watch and Harvard IHRC, Losing Humanity (19 Nov 2012) ( opens in a new tab ) hrw.org Two senses of "on" the EU 2019 ethics guidelines define on the loop as intervening during design and monitoring operation, which differs from the military override sense used here; the guidelines have no out-of-the-loop term 1 . Sources (1) EU High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (8 Apr 2019) ( opens in a new tab ) ec.europa.eu Approving to monitoring experienced users shift from approving individual actions to monitoring the agent and intervening when needed 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Out is a per-step property no source claims a person is out of the loop for a whole lifecycle; the humans move to specs and outcome checks 1 . Sources (1) Willison, How StrongDM's AI team build serious software without even looking at the code ( opens in a new tab ) simonwillison.net Regulation limits out for high-risk uses, EU AI Act Article 14 requires that a person can override and stop the system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Aviation supplied the concept, not the words Sheridan traces supervisory control to computers replacing direct manual control in aircraft, which left the person "in a new role of monitor and goal-constraint setter"; no source traces the words "in, on, out of the loop" to aviation, they come from the military policy above 1 . Sources (1) Sheridan, Human Supervisory Control (Handbook of Systems Engineering and Management, Wiley, 1999, ch. 16) ( opens in a new tab ) hlaszny.com Levels are not a strict ladder the FAA warns that describing automation as a linear hierarchy of levels is difficult to apply operationally, and that responsibility for flightpath management stays with the pilots at all times; it concerns airline pilots, so carrying it to agents is an analogy 1 . Sources (1) FAA, Advisory Circular 120-123, Flightpath Management (21 Nov 2022) ( opens in a new tab ) faa.gov

Trust lets you step out; review builds the trust Software is easy to check "Software is unusually amenable to supervisory oversight because the outputs can be tested"; where checking needs the expertise that producing took, trust may build more slowly 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice (18 Feb 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Vigilance is no check complacency and automation bias occur in naive and expert people and are not removed by training or instructions, so the check must be built into the result 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman and Manzey, Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration (Human Factors 52(3), 2010) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Level is a design choice the level of automation is set per function, judged by human performance consequences and the cost of errors, which is why a task may stay in for reasons other than checkability 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Oversight follows risk in the rules the EU AI Act requires oversight measures "commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use" of a high-risk system 1 . Sources (1) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), Article 14 Human oversight ( opens in a new tab ) artificialintelligenceact.eu Risk as a tool rating OpenAI tells builders to rate each tool low, medium or high by factors such as read-only versus write access, reversibility and financial impact, and to trigger human oversight for sensitive, irreversible or high-stakes actions until confidence in the agent grows 1 . Sources (1) OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents ( opens in a new tab ) cdn.openai.com Risk is one input, not the rule no source says risk alone decides the level; the aviation-derived model ranks the effect on human performance first and the cost of errors second, so combining risk and checkability into one per-task choice is a synthesis 1 . Sources (1) Parasuraman, Sheridan, Wickens, A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation (IEEE Trans. SMC-A 30(3), 2000) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org
What it requires of each person No speaker notes for this Slide.

Plan back from the goal Pappus and Pólya analysis starts from what is required, takes it for granted, and asks from what antecedent it could be derived, until it reaches something already known; Pólya’s entry calls it “working backwards” 1 . Sources (1) Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards ( opens in a new tab ) hlevkin.com Regression in planning in AI planning, each backward step adds the action’s preconditions to the goal, and each precondition is a dependency the plan needs 1 . Sources (1) Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning ( opens in a new tab ) aima.cs.berkeley.edu Fewer actions to consider backward search considers only relevant actions; in the textbook air cargo problem about 1000 actions lead forward and 20 work backward, for that one problem only 1 . Sources (1) Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 2nd ed., chapter 11 Planning ( opens in a new tab ) aima.cs.berkeley.edu It feels wrong Pólya notes a psychological difficulty in turning around and not following the direct path to the end 1 . Sources (1) Pólya, How to Solve It (1945), entries Pappus and Working backwards ( opens in a new tab ) hlevkin.com Project management does it too in the Critical Path Method, Kelley and Walker compute the latest time each event may occur “relative to a fixed project completion time”; neither this paper nor the NASA handbook uses the phrase “backward pass”, which is later textbook vocabulary 1 . Sources (1) Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959) ( opens in a new tab ) mosaicprojects.com.au What the backward run gives a job whose maximum available time equals its duration is critical, because a delay in it delays the project; the method takes the jobs and dependencies as given and is not shown to find missing tasks, so that use here is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Kelley and Walker, Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling (Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference, 1959) ( opens in a new tab ) mosaicprojects.com.au Scope starts at the end product the NASA handbook says a work breakdown structure begins with the end item and successively subdivides it, and calls it “a product-oriented structure, not an organizational structure” 1 . Sources (1) Sadler, NASA Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Handbook (NASA/SP-20250006071) ( opens in a new tab ) nasa.gov Vendors say: clear goals Anthropic names the best-fit tasks for agents as those with clear success criteria and feedback loops, such as code that automated tests can verify; this is guidance, not a measurement 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Missing detail costs accuracy models infer unstated requirements 41.1% of the time, prompts that omit requirements are twice as likely to regress when the model or prompt changes, and accuracy sometimes drops by more than 20% 1 . Sources (1) Yang et al., What Prompts Don’t Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Asking recovers it, and the limit on an underspecified coding benchmark, interacting to ask questions gained up to 74% over not asking, a ceiling and not an average; no source isolates a clear goal as a single variable, so the claim is that missing detail hurts and recovering it helps 1 . Sources (1) Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Contracts at the seams A contract has two sides Meyer’s model is the business contract: each party expects benefits and accepts obligations to obtain them, documented in a contract document 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu Pre- and postcondition the precondition states what any call must satisfy, the postcondition what the call ensures in return; each condition belongs to exactly one party 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu No defensive duplication either the condition is guaranteed by the client or handled by the supplier; checking everything on both sides adds complexity 1 . Sources (1) Meyer, Applying “Design by Contract” (IEEE Computer, October 1992) ( opens in a new tab ) pages.mtu.edu Same split in Eiffel Eiffel Software defines a precondition as what must be true before a component is used and a postcondition as what it guarantees after execution 1 . Sources (1) Eiffel Software, Design by Contract ( opens in a new tab ) eiffel.com

Reviewing the result Two definitions Boehm defines verification as establishing the correspondence between a software product and its specification, and validation as establishing its fitness or worth for its operational mission 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com His two questions “Am I building the product right?” for verification and “Am I building the right product?” for validation 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com Where the fix lands a failed verification changes the product; a failed validation can change the requirements themselves 1 . Sources (1) Boehm, Guidelines for Verifying and Validating Software Requirements and Design Specifications (Euro IFIP 79) ( opens in a new tab ) mferchaves.wordpress.com Software practice, not agents NASA words the same pair as “Are we building the product right?”; applying it to work handed to an agent is an inference 1 . Sources (1) NASA, IV&V Overview ( opens in a new tab ) nasa.gov
What it requires of the organisation No speaker notes for this Slide.

The org chart trap The law as Conway states it "Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure" 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, Conway's Law (author's page) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com Why it happens organising the team already makes design decisions, and two parts of a design can depend on each other only where their designers talked 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, How Do Committees Invent? (Datamation, April 1968) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com A tendency, not a rule a review of 142 empirical studies found mirroring a prevalent pattern but not universal: strong in 70% of industry and firm studies, absent in 56% of open collaborative projects 1 . Sources (1) Colfer and Baldwin, The mirroring hypothesis: theory, evidence, and exceptions (Industrial and Corporate Change, 2016) ( opens in a new tab ) dash.harvard.edu Components include tasks the same review defines the components of a technical system as all the tasks and decisions required to design, operate and maintain it 1 . Sources (1) Colfer and Baldwin, The mirroring hypothesis: theory, evidence, and exceptions (Industrial and Corporate Change, 2016) ( opens in a new tab ) dash.harvard.edu The first design is not the best Conway himself says the first design is almost never the best possible, so the organisation must stay flexible 1 . Sources (1) Melvin Conway, How Do Committees Invent? (Datamation, April 1968) ( opens in a new tab ) melconway.com

Designed AI first Checkpoints in the path Anthropic's agent guidance has agents pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when encountering blockers 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com Contract-first decomposition a delegation framework makes delegation contingent on the outcome having precise verification, and splits a subtask further when its output is too costly or subjective to verify 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Vague handoffs duplicate work Anthropic's research system produced duplicated work and gaps until each subagent had an objective, an output format, tool guidance and clear task boundaries 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

What to look for in your team Management 101 skills "If you can explain what you need, give effective feedback, and design ways of evaluating work, you are going to be able to work with agents" 1 . Sources (1) Mollick, Management as AI Superpower (One Useful Thing, 27 January 2026) ( opens in a new tab ) oneusefulthing.org Effort moves to steering and checking in a survey of 319 knowledge workers, critical thinking moved toward information verification, response integration and task stewardship 1 . Sources (1) Lee et al. (Carnegie Mellon, Microsoft Research), The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI 2025) ( opens in a new tab ) microsoft.com Evidence is indirect no source tests breaking work down, writing handoffs and reviewing results as a set, and none measures how many people can do them; that these are the skills to build is a synthesis 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Juniors may not build them the narrow tasks through which juniors build judgement are those most likely to be offloaded to agents 1 . Sources (1) Tomašev, Franklin, Osindero (Google DeepMind), Intelligent AI Delegation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

From article to quiz Workflow and agent, two levels Anthropic separates workflows, orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents that direct their own process; reading the quiz example as a path you design with steps the agent steers is an application of that split, not a claim the source makes 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Building effective agents ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

script.text: This panel shows the speaker notes and voice script for the Slide you are reading, and follows you as you scroll. Press Alt+N to open or close it.

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:24 Imagine the board Imagine you are the manager of a summer party for 200 colleagues from five offices, and you have hired four excellent freelancers to plan it, one each for Activities, Travel, Venue and Food and drinks. They never meet and they never call each other, because the only thing they share is a board where everyone leaves notes.

The thought experiment 0:00 – 0:21 Everyone delivered Now the day arrives, and every one of the four has done exactly what was asked. Activities booked a team-building event, Travel arranged how everyone gets there, Venue found a place, and Food and drinks ordered dinner. Each card is ticked, and each freelancer met their own goal perfectly. 0:21 – 1:14 None of it adds up And still the party fails, because the failures sit between the cards. Activities booked paintball, while Travel had booked an accessible bus for ten colleagues in wheelchairs, who now sit it out. Travel had everyone carpool, while Food and drinks booked an open bar until one in the morning, so the drivers have been drinking. Venue found a scenic alpine hut, while the guest info from Travel gives only route and times, so people arrive in summer clothes for six degrees at night. And dinner was ordered with 31 vegetarian, which the hut's kitchen reads the Western way, so egg dishes land in front of colleagues who cannot eat them. Every step was perfect, and perfect steps do not add up on their own. 1:14 – 1:46 Your question So here is the question, and I want you to keep it in your head for the whole Episode. What do you, as the manager, need to do so the result still comes out great? One tempting answer is to get the four talking, to hold more meetings. I will leave the question open for now, and we will answer it step by step, from different angles, until we collect the answers at the end.

Now with agents 0:00 – 0:21 Speed, not context Now give the same four cards to agents. Each card is ticked far faster, which is wonderful, and it is exactly where the trap sits. AI speeds up the doing, but it cannot add context that nobody gave it, and the paintball agent never saw the accessible bus. 0:21 – 0:50 Plausible guess What makes this worse is that an agent which finds a gap tends to fill it with a plausible guess, instead of stopping to ask you. Nobody told the food agent what vegetarian means for these colleagues, so it picks the most common reading and carries on. The same four failures appear in the same four places, only now you reach them in two minutes instead of two weeks.
What an agentic workflow is 0:00 – 0:12 Name the thing Before we fix the board, we need two terms to stand on. What is an agent, and what makes a workflow agentic? Term first, then the board.

What an agent is 0:00 – 0:23 Model, tools, loop An agent is a language model that uses tools in a loop and decides for itself how to reach a goal. It is not a single chat answer you read and move on from, it is a loop of acting, looking at the result and acting again until it believes it is done. 0:23 – 0:52 Steers its own steps If you have only used a chat tool so far, here is the shift. In a chat you steer every step yourself, because you read each answer and decide what to ask next. An agent steers its own steps, so you cannot assume it takes the steps you would have taken. That is the reason the rest of this Episode is about what you must set up around it.

What an agentic workflow is 0:00 – 0:15 The definition An agentic workflow is a process in which agents, not people, take the decisions and do the tasks, within a structure you set. The exact wording and where it comes from are in the Speaker notes. 0:15 – 0:35 Two levels Read it as two levels. On the first level you design the path, which means the tasks and what each task hands over to the next. On the second level the agent steers inside its own task, and that is the part you hand away. 0:35 – 0:48 Minimal, how minimal Notice the phrase minimal human intervention, because it carries a lot of weight and says very little. How minimal, and for which task? That is what the next Section answers.

How far you step out 0:00 – 0:18 Open question The definition left one thing open, which is how much of a person stays in the workflow. That is not one setting for the whole company, it is a choice you make for each task, and it is the next thing to learn.

In, on or out of the loop 0:00 – 0:15 In Human in the loop means the agent acts only after a person has approved. Take booking the venue for the party: the agent proposes a venue, and nothing is booked until you say yes. 0:15 – 0:31 On Human on the loop means the agent acts on its own while a person watches and can step in. Now the agent books the venue itself, you read its reports, and you step in when something looks wrong. 0:31 – 0:43 Out Human out of the loop means the agent acts without any person, who sees only the result. The agent books the venue, and all you get is the confirmation. 0:43 – 1:06 Borrowed terms These three terms were borrowed from automation outside AI, from fields where an automated action often cannot be undone, so what role the person plays was decided on purpose and not left to chance. The detail is in the Speaker notes. We borrow them because the question is the same for your agents. 1:06 – 1:17 Per task So you choose per task, not per company. Minimal intervention stops being a vague promise and becomes a setting that you choose, task by task.

Trust lets you step out; review builds the trust 0:00 – 0:20 The rule Trust is what lets you step out of the loop, and you only trust a result you can check. Where checking costs as much as doing the work yourself, stepping out does not save you anything, it only means you accept a risk that nobody looks at. 0:20 – 0:33 Hypothesis, said openly That rule is my hypothesis, and I say so openly; the evidence for it comes mostly from software, so treat it as a good bet and not as a law. 0:33 – 0:51 Review builds the trust So the engineering comes first: you build the check in before the agent starts, a test the result can pass. When it passes, that is evidence, and evidence is what builds the trust. A feeling that the agent is good does not. 0:51 – 1:09 Risk sets the bar Risk sets how much trust a task needs. The guest list needs little, a missing name is one email. The venue and the activity need a lot, because a wrong result can leave two hundred people at a place that does not fit. 1:09 – 1:31 The activity moves Now look at the activity. It needed trust three and had one, so a person stayed in. Give it its check, everyone can join, wheelchair access, no fitness needed, and once the check passes the trust is earned and the task moves from in the loop to on the loop.

What it requires of each person 0:00 – 0:18 Skills behind the failures Let's go back to the board. Each of the four failures came from a skill that was missing in a person, and there are three skills in all. Each one has a name, and we take them one at a time.

Plan back from the goal 0:00 – 0:22 Start at the goal Start with the goal and work backwards. Backward reasoning is a plain-language name for something Pólya calls working backwards and AI planning calls regression. You ask what must be true just before the goal, then what must be true before that, and you repeat until you arrive at where you stand today. 0:22 – 0:38 State the outcome Write the goal as an outcome and not as an activity. Not book a venue, but everyone celebrates together and gets home safely, because an outcome tells you when you are done and an activity does not. 0:38 – 0:57 Outside your control Next, sort what the plan depends on into what is inside your control and what is outside it. The venue's kitchen is not yours, you cannot change how it works, so you plan around it and make sure whatever you hand it is unmistakable. 0:57 – 1:32 The tasks nobody owned Now work back from gets home safely. Just before it, people need a ride home, and nobody had planned one after an open bar, so a shuttle appears on the board. Just before arrival, guests need to know what the night will be like, so the guest info gets a line saying bring warm clothes, six degrees at night. Those two tasks belonged to nobody on the first board, and with them the drinking drivers and the cold guests have an owner. 1:32 – 1:50 Well known, and agents like it Planning back from the goal is nothing exotic, and agents also do better when they receive a clearly defined goal and outcome. So when you hand a task to an agent, have you given it the goal, or only the activity?

Contracts at the seams 0:00 – 0:17 Design by contract Design by contract, after Meyer, says that cooperation rests on contracts, and a contract states what each party receives and what it delivers. That sounds like software, but it is the most practical tool a manager has for a handoff. 0:17 – 0:34 Receives, delivers, checked by So before you hand any task to an agent, write three lines. What it receives, what it must deliver, and how someone else can check the result. Do this for one task this week, before you hand it over. 0:34 – 0:57 Leave the how open Notice what the contract leaves out, and that is how the work is done. How the menu gets cooked is the kitchen's choice. That is my reading of design by contract, Meyer does not say it in these words, but it is why a contract stays short enough to write for every handoff. 0:57 – 1:18 The egg dishes Now the egg dishes. The fact 31 vegetarian travelled from one card to the other without a single error, but the word meant something else on each side. With a definition, no meat, fish or eggs, and a check of the menu against it, the egg dishes cannot arrive quietly.

Reviewing the result 0:00 – 0:11 Two checks Reviewing a result takes two checks that people often merge into one. Verification checks the result against its contract. Validation checks the result against the goal. 0:11 – 0:28 Paintball passes The paintball note passes every line of its contract: an activity for 200, within budget, on the right day. And it still fails the goal, because the contract was right about what was asked and wrong about what was needed. 0:28 – 0:46 The human part The second check is the human part, and it is the one that lets you step further out. When you are not watching, what you can trust is a result that has been checked against the goal, not only against the note. 0:46 – 0:57 Your verdict So the next time an agent hands you a result that matches its task perfectly, ask yourself which of the two checks you have actually done.

What it requires of the organisation 0:00 – 0:12 From people to the company Skills in your people are not enough. The workflow they draw has a shape of its own, and that shape comes from the organisation they work in.

The org chart trap 0:00 – 0:17 Conway's law Conway's law, from 1968, in plain words: what people design follows who talks to whom. A workflow that people draw for themselves is a design too, so it does the same. The exact wording is in the Speaker notes. 0:17 – 0:37 A team's draft I saw this with a team I worked with. They drew their AI workflow, and one discipline ended up with fourteen discovery steps while the others got one or two. The workflow mirrored the headcount, not the goal. I will not name the company or the team. 0:37 – 0:53 Broadly defined Conway meant systems in a wide sense, but applying that to workflows is my inference, because nobody has measured it for workflows. It explains what I saw, though, and it gives you a test you can run. 0:53 – 1:06 Your sign So if the workflow your people draw looks like your org chart, suspect Conway's law and redraw it from the goal. If you lead the transformation, that check is yours to make.

Designed AI first 0:00 – 0:17 Start at the outcome Here are three tips for a lean workflow, and the first is to start from the goal and its measurable outcome, not from today's roles. The roles tell you who is available, and the outcome tells you what is needed. 0:17 – 0:33 Contract on every milestone The second is to put a contract on every milestone and leave the inside of each step free. You decide what must arrive and how it is checked, and the person or the agent decides the rest. 0:33 – 0:44 Cut seams The third is to cut seams. Every seam is a place where a gap can hide, so merge the steps that produce nothing anyone can review. 0:44 – 0:56 Not more meetings Remember the question from the first Slide? One answer was to get them talking, to hold more meetings. You did not need more meetings, you needed contracts.

What to look for in your team 0:00 – 0:11 The answer So what did you need to do? You needed three skills in your people, and each one is tied to the failures it would have fixed. 0:11 – 0:23 Break down The first is to break the work down from the goal. Do that, and the drinking drivers and the cold guests have an owner before the party starts. 0:23 – 0:36 Write contracts The second is to write the contract at the seam, what a task receives, what it delivers and how it is checked. Do that, and the egg dishes cannot happen. 0:36 – 0:45 Review twice The third is to review twice, against the contract and against the goal. Do that, and the paintball does not go ahead. 0:45 – 0:59 The organisation The organisation has its own part: clear goals, contracts between teams, a policy on how much oversight each task gets, and workflows designed around the goal and not around the org chart. 0:59 – 1:16 Look at your team Now look at your team. Who can break work down, who writes a clear handoff, and who can review an agent's result? Those are the skills to build, and in my view they are where your effort pays off first. 1:16 – 1:33 Take one process And before Monday, do the smallest version of all of this. Pick one recurring process in your team, mark which steps an agent could run, and decide for each whether a person stays in, on or out of the loop.

From article to quiz 0:00 – 0:18 One whole workflow Let's put it all together in one whole agentic workflow. It takes any knowledge article, a PDF or a URL, and turns it into a quiz. The path of steps is yours to design, and each step is the agent's to steer. 0:18 – 0:46 In, on or out per step Each step gets its own level, in, on or out of the loop, set by the risk of a wrong result and by how well that result can be checked. You can do this with a process of your own: pick one recurring process in your team and mark which steps an agent could run, and whether a person stays in, on or out for each. 0:46 – 1:06 A contract at every handoff At every handoff sits a contract: what the next step receives, what it must deliver, and how someone else can check it. Write these three lines before you hand any task to an agent, and it is what lets you still trust what comes back. 1:06 – 1:42 Designed around the goal Notice where this workflow started, from the goal, a quiz someone can use, and not from how any team works today. If you lead a transformation and the workflow your people draw mirrors how they work now, suspect Conway's law and redraw it around the goal. And look at your team, because breaking work down, writing clear handoffs and reviewing an agent's result are the skills to build. Pick one process, write the contracts, decide the levels, and build those three skills in your people.
